questions.stem:
A school chemistry laboratory stocks steel cylinders of oxygen and nitrogen. The teacher points out that the atomic number of nitrogen is 7 and that the atomic number of oxygen is eight. She asks the class to work out how each atom completes its outer shell when two atoms of the same element join. One pair of nitrogen atoms shares three electrons each and is joined by three shared pairs of electrons. A pair of oxygen atoms behaves differently: each oxygen atom has six electrons in its L shell and requires two more to complete its octet, so each shares two electrons.

State how many electrons an oxygen atom has in its L shell and how many more it needs to complete its octet. (ii) State how many electrons each nitrogen atom contributes when the two nitrogen atoms join, and name the bond that is formed between them. (iii) Both elements form diatomic molecules in this way. Compare the two: state how many shared pairs of electrons each molecule contains and name the bond in each, and then explain what both kinds of atom gain by sharing electrons.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (i) Six; two more to complete the octet. (ii) Three electrons each; a triple bond. (iii) Nitrogen has three shared pairs and a triple bond, oxygen has two shared pairs and a double bond; in both the shared electrons belong to the outermost shells of both atoms, so each atom attains the noble gas configuration.

an atom of oxygen has six electrons
in its L shell (the atomic number of oxygen is eight) and it requires two
more electrons to complete its octet.

pairs of electrons. This is said to constitute a triple bond
between the two atoms.

questions.topic: Bonding in Carbon – the Covalent Bond
questions.stem:
In a school laboratory a student is asked to draw what happens when two hydrogen atoms meet. The atomic number of hydrogen is 1, so a hydrogen atom has a single electron in its K shell and needs one more to fill it. The two atoms therefore set their electrons in a shared pair, and the student is told that this shared pair of electrons constitutes a single covalent bond between the two hydrogen atoms. The teacher adds that the same bond can also be represented as a single straight line drawn between the two atoms.

State how many electrons a hydrogen atom has in its K shell and how many more it needs to fill that shell. (ii) Name the bond that the shared pair of electrons forms between the two hydrogen atoms, and state how the same bond can also be represented. (iii) Both hydrogen atoms end up with the electronic configuration of the same noble gas. Name that noble gas and explain, in terms of shared electrons, what each hydrogen atom gains.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (i) One electron; it needs one more. (ii) A single covalent bond; also as a line between the two atoms. (iii) Helium, which has two electrons in its K shell; the shared electrons belong to the outermost shells of both atoms, so each hydrogen atom attains the configuration of helium.

evidence:
hydrogen has one electron in its K shell and it requires one more electron
to fill the K shell.

The shared pair of electrons is said to constitute a
single covalent bond between the two hydrogen atoms.

electronic configuration of the nearest noble gas,
helium, which has two electrons in its K shell.

questions.topic: Bonding in Carbon – the Covalent Bond
questions.stem:
A city bus is fuelled by Compressed Natural Gas, and a kitchen in the same city burns methane on a gas stove. Both fuels depend on one of the simplest compounds formed by carbon. A student asks why carbon behaves so differently from the elements around it. The teacher explains that carbon has four electrons in its outermost shell, so it is tetravalent, and that in order to achieve noble gas configuration carbon shares these electrons with four atoms of hydrogen, whose valency is 1. Gaining or losing four electrons, the teacher adds, is not practical for carbon.

State why carbon is called tetravalent, and give the valency of hydrogen. (ii) State with how many atoms of hydrogen a carbon atom shares its electrons in methane, and say what configuration the carbon atom thereby attains. (iii) The teacher says carbon could have gained four electrons or lost four electrons instead of sharing them, but that neither route works. Give the reason carbon cannot simply gain four electrons, and give the reason losing four electrons is not practical.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (i) Carbon has four valence electrons; hydrogen has a valency of 1. (ii) Four atoms of hydrogen; it attains noble gas configuration. (iii) Its nucleus has six protons, so holding ten electrons would be difficult; removing four electrons would need a large amount of energy and would leave a carbon cation holding just two electrons.

electrons.

questions.subject: Science
questions.topic: Some Important Carbon Compounds – Ethanol and Ethanoic Acid
questions.stem:
A student in a school chemistry laboratory is asked to name two carbon compounds. The first is a three-carbon chain carrying a ketone group; the student is told to delete the final ‘e’ of the chain name before adding the ending of the functional group. The second is an unsaturated three-carbon chain, and the student is told that the ending ‘ane’ must be replaced by ‘ene’ or ‘yne’ instead. The teacher then burns a sample of carbon in oxygen and reminds the class that most carbon compounds behave in the same way on burning.

State the suffix used for a ketone group and give the name of the compound formed when a three-carbon chain carries that group, showing how the chain name changes. (ii) The teacher then burns a sample of carbon in oxygen and says most carbon compounds behave in the same way. State the gas that carbon gives off and the two things released along with it, and explain what this leads a student to expect when a carbon compound burns.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (i) The suffix is ‘one’; the final ‘e’ of propane is deleted to leave propan, and adding ‘one’ gives propanone. (ii) Carbon dioxide, with heat and light. Most carbon compounds also release a large amount of heat and light on burning, and these are oxidation reactions, so a compound gives off the same two things.

evidence:
the name of the carbon chain is modified by deleting the final ‘e’ and
adding the appropriate suffix. For example, a three-carbon chain
with a ketone group would be named in the following manner –
Propane – ‘e’ = propan + ‘one’ = propanone.
